claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute the largest family of integral membrane proteins in human genome with over 800 members.
source: With over 800 members, GPCRs constitute the largest family of integral membrane proteins in human genome and represent roughly half of all drug targets in modern medicine (Gilchrist, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gilchrist, 2010.

claim: GPCRs represent roughly half of all drug targets in modern medicine.
source: With over 800 members, GPCRs constitute the largest family of integral membrane proteins in human genome and represent roughly half of all drug targets in modern medicine (Gilchrist, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gilchrist, 2010.

claim: The human β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR) is expressed in pulmonary and cardiac myocyte tissues.
source: It is expressed in pulmonary and cardiac myocyte tissues and is a therapeutic target for asthma and heart failure (Lefkowitz, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefkowitz, 2000.

claim: β2AR is a therapeutic target for asthma and heart failure.
source: It is expressed in pulmonary and cardiac myocyte tissues and is a therapeutic target for asthma and heart failure (Lefkowitz, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lefkowitz, 2000.

claim: The functional diversity of β2AR is associated with its structural dynamics.
source: The functional diversity of β2AR is associated with its structural dynamics (Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manglik and Kobilka, 2014 and Kobilka, 2013.

claim: Structures of β2AR in the inactive and active states have provided valuable insights into the structure-function relationship of β2AR.
source: Recently found structures of β2AR in the inactive and active states have provided valuable insights into the structure-function relationship of β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008; Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008; Rasmussen et al., 2011.

claim: Biophysical and biochemical studies have provided direct evidences of multiple distinct conformational states for specific GPCRs, such as β2AR.
source: Subsequent biophysical and biochemical studies have provided direct evidences of multiple distinct conformational states for specific GPCRs, such as β2AR (Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013; Nygaard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013; Nygaard et al., 2013.

claim: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have depicted the dynamic behavior of β2AR and have significantly enhanced our understanding of the activation mechanism of GPCRs.
source: Meanwhile, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have depicted the dynamic behavior of β2AR and have significantly enhanced our understanding of the activation mechanism of GPCRs (Dror et al., 2009; Ozcan et al., 2013; Dror et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dror et al., 2009; Ozcan et al., 2013; Dror et al., 2011.

claim: The activation of GPCRs is modulated by lipids.
source: Intriguingly, it is now evident that the activation of GPCRs is modulated by lipids (Oates and Watts, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oates and Watts, 2011.

claim: The COPI machinery protein p24 is recognized by a specific sphingomyelin.
source: Contreras et al. showed that the COPI machinery protein p24 is recognized by a specific sphingomyelin (Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Contreras et al., 2012.

claim: Monosialoganglioside GM3 influences the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor.
source: Coskun et al. showed that monosialoganglioside GM3 influences the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (Coskun et al., 2011), however the mechanism is not known.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coskun et al., 2011.

claim: The mechanism by which monosialoganglioside GM3 influences the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor is not known.
source: Coskun et al. showed that monosialoganglioside GM3 influences the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (Coskun et al., 2011), however the mechanism is not known.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statement 'however the mechanism is not known' following the citation.

claim: Lipid modulation holds to GPCRs in particular through cholesterol.
source: Lipid modulation also holds to GPCRs (Oates and Watts, 2011; Neale et al., 2015; Dawaliby et al., 2016) in particular through cholesterol (Oates and Watts, 2011; Paila and Chattopadhyay, 2009; Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Muth et al., 2011), which changes the physical properties of cellular membranes and supports the dynamic assembly of nanoscale membrane domains (Simons and Ikonen, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations including Oates and Watts, 2011; Paila and Chattopadhyay, 2009; Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Muth et al., 2011.

claim: Cholesterol changes the physical properties of cellular membranes and supports the dynamic assembly of nanoscale membrane domains.
source: Lipid modulation also holds to GPCRs (Oates and Watts, 2011; Neale et al., 2015; Dawaliby et al., 2016) in particular through cholesterol (Oates and Watts, 2011; Paila and Chattopadhyay, 2009; Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Muth et al., 2011), which changes the physical properties of cellular membranes and supports the dynamic assembly of nanoscale membrane domains (Simons and Ikonen, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Simons and Ikonen, 2000.

claim: β2AR belongs to the family of class A GPCRs.
source: β2AR belongs to the family of class A GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: GPCRs belonging to class A show a high structural similarity and functional diversity.
source: GPCRs belonging to this class show a high structural similarity and functional diversity.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Cholesterol affects the conformation of many GPCRs.
source: It has been experimentally shown that cholesterol affects the conformation (Muth et al., 2011; Casiraghi et al., 2016) and function (Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Pucadyil and Chattopadhyay, 2006; Casiraghi et al., 2016; Jafurulla et al., 2014) of many GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Muth et al., 2011; Casiraghi et al., 2016.

claim: Cholesterol affects the function of many GPCRs.
source: It has been experimentally shown that cholesterol affects the conformation (Muth et al., 2011; Casiraghi et al., 2016) and function (Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Pucadyil and Chattopadhyay, 2006; Casiraghi et al., 2016; Jafurulla et al., 2014) of many GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gimpl et al., 1997; Paila et al., 2011; Pucadyil and Chattopadhyay, 2006; Casiraghi et al., 2016; Jafurulla et al., 2014.

claim: Based on X-ray crystal structures cholesterol has specific contacts with β2AR.
source: Based on X-ray crystal structures cholesterol has specific contacts with β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008), suggesting that β2AR has binding sites for cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008.

claim: β2AR has binding sites for cholesterol.
source: Based on X-ray crystal structures cholesterol has specific contacts with β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008), suggesting that β2AR has binding sites for cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is inferred from X-ray crystal structures showing specific contacts.

claim: Spectroscopic and MD simulation studies have reported direct interactions between cholesterol and GPCRs, including β2AR.
source: Spectroscopic (Gater et al., 2014) and MD simulation (Cang et al., 2013; Prasanna et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012) studies have reported direct interactions between cholesterol and GPCRs, including β2AR.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gater et al., 2014; Cang et al., 2013; Prasanna et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Cholesterol binding to β2AR changes its structural properties.
source: Experimental data show that cholesterol binding to β2AR changes its structural properties (Hanson et al., 2008; Zocher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hanson et al., 2008; Zocher et al., 2012.

claim: Cholesterol is necessary in crystallizing β2AR.
source: Cholesterol is also necessary in crystallizing β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008), and cholesterol and its analogue cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) have been exhibited to improve β2AR stability (Zocher et al., 2012; Loll, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008.

claim: Cholesterol and its analogue cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) have been exhibited to improve β2AR stability.
source: Cholesterol is also necessary in crystallizing β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008), and cholesterol and its analogue cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) have been exhibited to improve β2AR stability (Zocher et al., 2012; Loll, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zocher et al., 2012; Loll, 2014.

claim: Cholesterol has a functional role in β2AR.
source: Indeed experimental studies indicate that cholesterol has a functional role in β2AR (Paila et al., 2011; Pontier et al., 2008; Xiang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paila et al., 2011; Pontier et al., 2008; Xiang et al., 2002.

claim: Inhibition of β2AR-associated signaling has been observed with increasing membrane cholesterol content.
source: Further, inhibition of β2AR-associated signaling has been observed with increasing membrane cholesterol content (Pontier et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pontier et al., 2008.

claim: The atomic-scale mechanism cholesterol uses to regulate β2AR is not known.
source: However, as with GPCRs in general, the atomic-scale mechanism cholesterol uses to regulate β2AR is not known.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a knowledge gap.

claim: Extensive atomistic MD simulations totaling >100 μs were performed to clarify the mechanism responsible for the modulatory role of cholesterol on β2AR.
source: We performed extensive atomistic MD simulations (totaling >100 μs, Table 1) to clarify the mechanism responsible for the modulatory role of cholesterol on β2AR.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Table 1.

claim: As cholesterol concentration reaches ~10 mol%, the conformational distribution of β2AR is drastically altered.
source: In essence, we show that as cholesterol concentration reaches ~10 mol%, the conformational distribution of β2AR is drastically altered.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The mechanism of action of cholesterol on β2AR is based on the binding of cholesterol at specific high-affinity sites located near the transmembrane helices 5–7 of the receptor.
source: The mechanism of action is based on the binding of cholesterol at specific high-affinity sites located near the transmembrane helices 5–7 of the receptor.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The alternative mechanism, where the β2AR conformation would be modulated by membrane-mediated interactions, plays only a minor role.
source: The alternative mechanism, where the β2AR conformation would be modulated by membrane-mediated interactions, plays only a minor role.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: Cholesterol analogues also bind to cholesterol binding sites and impede the structural flexibility of β2AR.
source: Cholesterol analogues also bind to cholesterol binding sites and impede the structural flexibility of β2AR, however cholesterol generates the strongest effect.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: Cholesterol generates the strongest effect on β2AR structural flexibility compared to cholesterol analogues.
source: Cholesterol analogues also bind to cholesterol binding sites and impede the structural flexibility of β2AR, however cholesterol generates the strongest effect.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: Helices 5–6 (H5-H6) constitute a highly dynamic region of β2AR.
source: Crystallographic studies and previous biophysical and biochemical studies have shown that helices 5–6 (H5-H6) (Figure 1A) constitute a highly dynamic region of β2AR (Kobilka, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobilka, 2013.

claim: Upon activation, the most dramatic conformational change in β2AR is a 7–14 Å outward movement of the intracellular end of H6 from the heptahelical core of the receptor.
source: Upon activation, the most dramatic conformational change, which is conserved among many GPCRs, is a 7–14 Å outward movement of the intracellular end of H6 from the heptahelical core of the receptor (Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013.

claim: The outward movement of the intracellular end of H6 upon activation is conserved among many GPCRs.
source: Upon activation, the most dramatic conformational change, which is conserved among many GPCRs, is a 7–14 Å outward movement of the intracellular end of H6 from the heptahelical core of the receptor (Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manglik and Kobilka, 2014; Kobilka, 2013.

claim: In a conformational change from the inactive to the active state β2AR, H5 (around S2075.46) has been found to move inward by 2 Å.
source: In a conformational change from the inactive to the active state β2AR, H5 (around S2075.46) has been found to move inward by 2 Å to establish an optimal interaction between the agonist and the two anchor sites (D1133.32/N3127.39 and S2035.42/S2045.43/S2075.46) on the receptor (Kobilka, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobilka, 2013.

claim: In a cholesterol-free DOPC bilayer, β2AR adopts a wide range of conformations with LL varying between ~11.5–17.5 Å and LG ranging between ~7.5–12.5 Å.
source: In a cholesterol-free DOPC bilayer, we find β2AR to adopt a wide range of conformations with LL varying between ~11.5–17.5 Å and LG ranging between ~7.5–12.5 Å (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing the conformational distribution.

claim: In a cholesterol-free DOPC bilayer, β2AR populates two major conformational states.
source: The receptor populates two major conformational states.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: One major conformational state of β2AR in cholesterol-free DOPC has a relatively open G protein site (LG being 10–12 Å) and a smaller ligand-binding site (LL ~ 13 ± 1 Å).
source: One of them has a relatively open G protein site (LG being 10–12 Å) and a smaller ligand-binding site (LL ~ 13 ± 1 Å).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The other major conformational state of β2AR in cholesterol-free DOPC is characterized by a shift of ~3–4 Å from the intracellular end of H6 towards the receptor core that blocks the G protein interface (LG ~ 8.5 Å).
source: The other conformation is characterized by a shift of ~3–4 Å from the intracellular end of H6 towards the receptor core that blocks the G protein interface (LG ~ 8.5 Å).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: In the alternative inactive conformation of β2AR, the ligand-binding pocket expands as the extracellular part of H5 moves ~ 4–5 Å away from H3 (LL now ~16 ± 1 Å).
source: At the same time, the ligand-binding pocket expands as the extracellular part of H5 moves ~ 4–5 Å away from H3 (LLnow ~16 ± 1 Å).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The alternative inactive conformation of β2AR represents an alternative inactive structure of the receptor, as both changes occur in the opposite direction compared to the case of agonist binding.
source: This conformation represents an alternative inactive structure of the receptor, as both changes occur in the opposite direction compared to the case of agonist binding (Kobilka, 2013); we do not observe any transition to the active state of β2AR.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data and a citation to Kobilka, 2013.

claim: No transition to the active state of β2AR was observed in the simulations.
source: This conformation represents an alternative inactive structure of the receptor, as both changes occur in the opposite direction compared to the case of agonist binding (Kobilka, 2013); we do not observe any transition to the active state of β2AR.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The closing of the intracellular G protein-binding surface is found to correlate with the opening of the extracellular ligand-binding pocket, and vice-versa.
source: The closing of the intracellular G protein-binding surface is found to correlate with the opening of the extracellular ligand-binding pocket, and vice-versa (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1D showing time evolution data.

claim: The conformational correlation between the two distal sites supports the view of allosteric regulation in GPCRs.
source: The conformational correlation between the two distal sites supports the view of allosteric regulation in GPCRs (Kobilka, 2013; Ozcan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations to Kobilka, 2013; Ozcan et al., 2013.

claim: With a cholesterol concentration of 10 mol%, the conformational flexibility of β2AR reduces significantly.
source: With a cholesterol concentration of 10 mol%, the conformational flexibility of β2AR reduces significantly (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing the conformational distribution.

claim: In the presence of 10 mol% cholesterol, the receptor stays predominantly in one conformation and no further opening of the ligand-binding site or the opening/closing of the G protein-binding site is observed.
source: The receptor stays predominantly in one conformation and no further opening of the ligand-binding site or the opening/closing of the G protein-binding site is observed, unlike in a cholesterol-free membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: With 10 mol% cholesterol, LL and LG fluctuate around ~13 and~9.5 Å, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, LL and LG fluctuate around ~13 and~9.5 Å, respectively.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing time evolution data.

claim: The slowing down of the movements of H5 and H6 correlates with the observed high-density spots of cholesterol at these helices (IC2 and EC1).
source: The slowing down of the movements of H5 and H6 correlates with the observed high-density spots of cholesterol at these helices (IC2 and EC1 in Figure 2 discussed in detail below).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2 showing cholesterol density.

claim: The deviations of H5 and H6 from their respective average positions are much smaller when they are bound to cholesterol.
source: The data show that the deviations of these helices from their respective average positions are much smaller when they are bound to cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1F showing standard deviation data.

claim: The effect of cholesterol on reducing helix deviations is particularly strong for the extracellular end of H5 at the ligand-binding site and for the intracellular end of H6 at the G protein-binding site.
source: The effect is particularly strong for the extracellular end of H5 at the ligand-binding site and for the intracellular end of H6 at the G protein-binding site.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The restricted dynamics of β2AR is also observed at higher cholesterol concentrations (25 and 40 mol%).
source: The restricted dynamics of β2AR is also observed at higher cholesterol concentrations (25 and 40 mol%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: At 25 and 40 mol% cholesterol, the receptor samples a similar conformational space as observed with 10 mol% cholesterol.
source: In these cases, the receptor samples a similar conformational space as observed with 10 mol% cholesterol.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: At lower cholesterol concentrations (2 and 5 mol%), the distribution of the receptor's conformation is much wider.
source: At lower concentrations (2 and 5 mol%), the distribution of the receptor's conformation is much wider (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: When the membrane contains a very small percentage of cholesterol (2 mol%), the range of conformations accessible to β2AR is almost comparable to that of a cholesterol-free membrane.
source: Particularly when the membrane contains a very small percentage of cholesterol (2 mol%), the range of conformations accessible to β2AR is almost comparable to that of a cholesterol-free membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: In the active state, the intracellular end of H6 is splayed outward from the helical bundle, providing room for the G protein.
source: In the active state, the intracellular end of H6 is splayed outward from the helical bundle, providing room for the G protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3A showing the active state structure.

claim: Inward swinging of H6 towards H3 is observed in the absence of cholesterol in the active state β2AR (which occurred in two out of three replica simulations).
source: We observe inward swinging of H6 towards H3 in the absence of cholesterol (which occurred in two out of three replica simulations).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The intracellular end of H6 spontaneously approaches H3 with LG dropping from 18.97 Å in the starting active conformation to ~11.5 Å in the absence of cholesterol.
source: As shown in Figure 3B,E, the intracellular end of H6 spontaneously approaches H3 with LG dropping from 18.97 Å in the starting active conformation to ~11.5 Å that is comparable to the crystallographically observed inactive conformation of β2AR (LG ~ 11 Å) (Hanson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3B,E showing structural changes and a citation to Hanson et al., 2008.

claim: Spontaneous deactivation of the receptor in the absence of the intracellular binding partner and cholesterol is in agreement with recent simulations and experimental studies.
source: Such spontaneous deactivation of the receptor in the absence of the intracellular binding partner and cholesterol is in agreement with recent simulations (Dror et al., 2011; Neale et al., 2015) and experimental studies (Rosenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations to Dror et al., 2011; Neale et al., 2015; Rosenbaum et al., 2011.

claim: With 40 mol% cholesterol, the active-like open conformation of β2AR is stable during the simulations.
source: Meanwhile, with 40 mol% cholesterol, we observe that the active-like open conformation is stable during the simulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: With 40 mol% cholesterol, the LG value remains stable around 16.5 Å and no deactivation is observed.
source: As shown in Figure 3C,E, the LG value remains stable around 16.5 Å and no deactivation is observed unlike in cholesterol-free systems.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3C,E showing time evolution data.

claim: A high cholesterol density is found at the intracellular segments of H5-H6 (IC2) in the active state β2AR with 40 mol% cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, here again we found a high cholesterol density at the intracellular segments of H5-H6 (IC2 in Figure 3C,D,F as discussed in detail below).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D,F showing cholesterol density.

claim: Cholesterol restricts the intrinsic conformation dynamics of β2AR and governs changes between different conformational states, thereby modulating its function.
source: These results show that cholesterol restricts the intrinsic conformation dynamics of β2AR and governs changes between different conformational states, thereby modulating its function.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: Cholesterol is observed to diffuse spontaneously to the receptor's surface in all simulations.
source: In all of the simulations (Table 1), cholesterol is observed to diffuse spontaneously to the receptor's surface.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: Time-averaged two-dimensional (2D) number density maps demonstrate that there are preferred cholesterol positions around β2AR.
source: Time-averaged two-dimensional (2D) number density maps demonstrate that there are preferred cholesterol positions around β2AR (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2A,B showing density maps.

claim: Three cholesterol interaction sites are identified in β2AR – two on the intracellular side (IC1 and IC2) and one on the extracellular side (EC1).
source: We identify three such cholesterol interaction sites – two on the intracellular side (IC1 and IC2) and one on the extracellular side (EC1) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: IC1, IC2, and EC1 are called high-affinity sites since they reproducibly exhibit high cholesterol densities (normalized number density above 0.7) at different cholesterol concentrations.
source: Here we call them high-affinity sites since they reproducibly exhibit high cholesterol densities (normalized number density above 0.7) at different cholesterol concentrations (Figure 2A,B) and also have large lifetimes as the below discussion shows.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2A,B showing density data.

claim: IC1 is a shallow groove formed by the intracellular parts of transmembrane helices H1-H4 and coincides well with the location of cholesterol observed in the crystal structure of β2AR.
source: IC1 is a shallow groove formed by the intracellular parts of transmembrane helices H1-H4 and coincides well with the location of cholesterol observed in the crystal structure of β2AR (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data and citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008.

claim: In IC2 cholesterol penetrates deep into the cleft between H5 and H6 on the intracellular side.
source: In IC2 cholesterol penetrates deep into the cleft between H5 and H6 on the intracellular side.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: A high density of cholesterol is observed at IC2 not only in the inactive but also in the active β2AR conformation.
source: A high density of cholesterol is observed at IC2 not only in the inactive but also in the active β2AR conformation (Figure 3C,D,F), which suggests that this site is biologically important.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 3C,D,F showing density data.

claim: The high density of cholesterol at IC2 in both inactive and active β2AR conformations suggests that this site is biologically important.
source: A high density of cholesterol is observed at IC2 not only in the inactive but also in the active β2AR conformation (Figure 3C,D,F), which suggests that this site is biologically important.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of high cholesterol density at IC2 in both conformations.

claim: EC1 is comprised of two closely spaced cholesterol hot spots located in the extracellular part of H5-H6 and H6-ECL3-H7.
source: EC1 is comprised of two closely spaced cholesterol hot spots located in the extracellular part of H5-H6 and H6-ECL3-H7 (where ECL stands for the extracellular loop).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The occupancy of two cholesterol molecules at EC1 is in good agreement with the crystal structure of the adenosine receptor A2AAR.
source: The occupancy of two cholesterol molecules at EC1 is in good agreement with the crystal structure of the adenosine receptor A2AAR (Liu et al., 2012), while IC2 is so far unidentified among the experimentally determined structures (Gater et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: IC2 is so far unidentified among the experimentally determined structures.
source: The occupancy of two cholesterol molecules at EC1 is in good agreement with the crystal structure of the adenosine receptor A2AAR (Liu et al., 2012), while IC2 is so far unidentified among the experimentally determined structures (Gater et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by a citation to Gater et al., 2014.

claim: The cholesterol binding residues of the three interaction sites (IC1, IC2, EC1) are conserved to a large degree among β2AR orthologues.
source: Notably, the cholesterol binding residues of the three interaction sites are conserved to a large degree among β2AR orthologues (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that these sites have conserved during the evolution of the receptor.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 showing sequence alignment data.

claim: The conservation of cholesterol binding residues indicates that these sites have conserved during the evolution of the receptor.
source: Notably, the cholesterol binding residues of the three interaction sites are conserved to a large degree among β2AR orthologues (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that these sites have conserved during the evolution of the receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the conservation of cholesterol binding residues.

claim: A few comparatively low-affinity cholesterol binding sites (IC3-4, EC2-3) with 10 and 40 mol% cholesterol are observed.
source: In addition, a few comparatively low-affinity cholesterol binding sites (IC3-4, EC2-3) with 10 and 40 mol% cholesterol are observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When cholesterol concentration is lowered below 10 mol%, many of the interaction sites, particularly IC1 and EC1, are occupied by cholesterol at concentrations as low as 5 mol%.
source: When cholesterol concentration is lowered below 10 mol%, many of the interaction sites, particularly IC1 and EC1, are occupied by cholesterol at concentrations as low as 5 mol% (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: A few sites (IC2 and EC1) are visited, though transiently, by cholesterol even at 2 mol%.
source: A few sites (IC2 and EC1) are visited, though transiently, by cholesterol even at 2 mol% (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Cholesterol binds to β2AR in specific binding sites.
source: Concluding, we find cholesterol to bind to β2AR in specific binding sites.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The cholesterol binding sites identified in simulations are in agreement with those found in the crystallographic structures of GPCRs.
source: These sites are in agreement with those found in the crystallographic structures of GPCRs (Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008; Gimpl, 2016; Warne et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Gater et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Hanson et al., 2008; Gimpl, 2016; Warne et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Gater et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in physical membrane properties, similar to those induced by cholesterol, do not restrict the conformational dynamics of β2AR.
source: Summarizing, the changes in physical membrane properties, similar to those induced by cholesterol, do not restrict the conformational dynamics of β2AR.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by simulation data.

claim: The cause of the observed changes in β2AR conformation and dynamics is the specific binding of cholesterol to β2AR.
